title: What Actually Happens Between Typing a URL and Seeing a Page
content:
Try this experiment sometime: type “google.com” into your browser, press Enter, and just… watch the loading spinner. Half a second, maybe less. In that blink of time, your request has traveled across the planet, been questioned by strangers, encrypted, decrypted, routed through machines you’ll never see, and answered by a small army of servers working in perfect coordination. Then it forgets all of that ever happened and just shows you a search box.

This is one of those interview questions every engineer eventually runs into — “walk me through what happens when you type a URL and hit Enter” — and it has a reputation for separating people who’ve memorized a framework from people who actually understand what’s underneath it. Not because it’s a trick question. Because it’s honest. It asks: do you know what you’re standing on?

One tip before we dive in, if you’re ever asked this live: ask your interviewer what they care about most. A front-end interviewer might want you to linger on how the browser renders the DOM. Someone hiring for infrastructure might want you to go deep on load balancing and failover. Asking that question first isn’t stalling — it’s exactly the kind of instinct a senior engineer has.

Now let’s actually follow the journey.

First, your browser has to figure out where “Google” even is

Here’s something people forget: computers don’t know what “google.com” means. Not even a little. Machines talk in numbers — IP addresses, things like 142.250.somewhere.14 — and “google.com” is just a friendly nickname we invented because nobody wants to memorize strings of digits for every website they visit.

So the browser’s very first move is a lookup, and it’s lazy in the best way — it checks the easiest, closest source first. Has it visited this site recently? Check the browser’s own cache. Not there? Ask the operating system, which keeps its own small memory of recent lookups. Still nothing? Now it goes further out, to a DNS resolver — usually run by your internet provider, or a public one like Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 or Google’s own 8.8.8.8.

If even that resolver doesn’t know the answer, it kicks off a small relay race across the internet’s backbone: first to a root server, which basically says “I don’t know Google’s address, but I know who manages all the .com domains — go ask them.” That .com server then points to Google’s own official name server, which finally hands back the real answer: an IP address. The whole thing usually takes single-digit milliseconds, and the internet is polite enough to cache the answer so it doesn’t have to repeat this dance every time.

Then two computers have to agree to talk

Having an address isn’t the same as having a conversation. Before any actual data moves, your computer and Google’s server need to establish a reliable connection — and this is where TCP/IP comes in.

Think of IP as the postal service: it’s responsible for getting a packet from point A to point B, hopping through routers along the way, figuring out the path. TCP is the layer that makes sure nothing gets lost or scrambled in transit — it’s the part that says “I sent you five packets, did you get all five, in order, undamaged?”

Before any real data flows, there’s a small ritual called the three-way handshake. Your machine sends a SYN, essentially saying “I’d like to talk.” The server replies SYN-ACK — “I hear you, and I’m listening.” Your machine sends back an ACK — “Great, let’s go.” Only after this tiny exchange is the connection considered open.

Somewhere in there, a gatekeeper checks your ID

Along this whole path, your traffic almost certainly passes through at least one firewall — maybe your home router’s, definitely something on Google’s side before your request ever touches their real infrastructure.

A firewall is exactly what it sounds like conceptually: a barrier that inspects traffic and decides what’s allowed through and what isn’t. Some firewalls just look at the outside of the packet — where it’s from, what port it’s headed to. Smarter ones actually inspect the content of the traffic, looking for patterns that smell like an attack. Either way, this is the internet’s immune system quietly doing its job in the background, and most of us never think about it until something gets blocked.

Then things get locked up tight

Because we typed “https” and not “http,” your browser insists on encryption before it’ll say another word. This is TLS — most people still call it SSL out of habit, even though SSL is technically its retired predecessor.

Right after the TCP handshake, there’s a second, more elaborate handshake — the TLS handshake. Google’s server presents a certificate, essentially a notarized ID card proving “yes, I really am google.com,” issued by an authority your browser already trusts. Both sides then do a clever bit of math to agree on a shared secret key, without ever actually sending that key across the wire in a way anyone could intercept. From that point forward, everything — your search terms, your cookies, everything — is scrambled into unreadable noise to anyone eavesdropping on the network.

This is genuinely one of the more elegant ideas in computer science: two strangers, on an open network, agreeing on a secret without ever whispering it out loud.

Your request arrives, but not at “a” server — at thousands of them

Google doesn’t run on one computer sitting in a room somewhere. It runs on a staggering number of machines spread across data centers on every continent. So your encrypted request doesn’t land on a specific server — it lands on a load balancer first.

Think of it like the host at a busy restaurant deciding which server should take your table — except the load balancer is also constantly checking which servers are overloaded, which ones just went down for maintenance, and which one happens to be physically closest to you to save a few milliseconds. It spreads traffic around so no single machine buckles under pressure, and if one server has a bad day, your request quietly gets rerouted to a healthy one without you ever noticing.

The web server picks up the phone

Now your request finally reaches an actual machine running web server software — something like Nginx or Apache in most companies, though Google runs its own custom-built version of this idea at massive scale.

The web server’s job here is more like a receptionist than a decision-maker. It handles the incoming HTTP request, deals with things like compression and the tail end of that encryption handshake, and figures out whether it can answer directly — say, for a simple static file — or whether it needs to pass the question to someone with actual authority to answer it.

For something as dynamic as a Google search, it definitely needs to pass it along.

This is where the actual thinking happens

That “someone with authority” is the application server, and this is genuinely the brain of the operation. This is the layer running the real logic — for a search engine, that means taking your query, running it through ranking systems, factoring in personalization, filtering, ads, and dozens of other signals, and figuring out what you should actually see.

If the web server is the receptionist, the application server is the expert who actually does the work you came in for. This is the layer most backend engineers spend their careers writing code for — the rules, the logic, the decisions.

But even the smartest logic needs somewhere to look things up

None of that decision-making happens in a vacuum — the application server needs data, and that data lives in databases. Sometimes that’s a classic relational database, sometimes a distributed system built to handle unthinkable scale, and in Google’s case, custom-built indexing systems designed specifically to search through more information than any human could comprehend.

The application server queries these databases, pulls back what it needs — search results, rankings, cached data — and assembles it all into a response.

And then, the whole thing runs in reverse

The response travels back the way it came: through the application server, through the web server, back out through the load balancer, re-encrypted across that same TLS tunnel, chopped back into TCP packets, and delivered to your browser. From there, your browser parses the HTML, fetches additional pieces like images and scripts (often triggering little versions of this entire journey all over again for each one), builds the page structure, and finally paints it on your screen.

DNS, TCP/IP, firewalls, encryption, load balancing, web servers, application logic, databases — eight completely different systems, built by different teams, running different technology, somehow cooperating flawlessly, all in less time than it takes to blink.

Why interviewers still love this question

It’s not really about testing memorization. It’s about testing whether you can zoom out — whether you understand that the app you’re building tomorrow doesn’t exist in isolation, but sits on top of decades of infrastructure that mostly just works, quietly, in the background. Understanding this stack, even at a surface level, tends to make people better engineers no matter which layer they eventually specialize in.

So next time someone asks you this in an interview — don’t panic. You already know the story. You just lived it, in half a second, the last time you opened a browser.

title: Mutable, Immutable… Everything is an Object in Python!
content:
A deep dive into one of Python’s most fundamental and misunderstood concepts — written for developers who want to truly understand what happens under the hood.

Introduction

If you have been writing Python for any amount of time, you have almost certainly encountered a moment of confusion: you pass a list to a function, the function modifies it, and when you come back to your original variable — it has changed too. Or perhaps you tried to modify a string character by character, only to be met with a cryptic TypeError. These behaviors are not bugs or quirks. They are the direct result of one of Python's most elegant and important design philosophies: everything in Python is an object, and every object is either mutable or immutable.

Unlike lower-level languages such as C or Java, where primitive types like integers, booleans, and characters are simple raw values stored directly in memory, Python treats absolutely everything as a fully-fledged object — complete with an identity, a type, and a value. Whether you write the number 42, the string "hello", a list, a dictionary, or even None and True, Python creates an object in memory for it. This unified object model is one of the reasons Python code feels so clean and consistent — but it also means you need to understand how these objects behave, especially when they are passed around, copied, or modified. That is exactly what this article is about.

id() and type() — Getting to Know Your Objects

Every single object in Python has three core properties: an identity, a type, and a value. Python gives you two built-in functions to inspect the first two: id() and type().

The id() function returns a unique integer that represents the memory address of the object. As long as the object exists in memory, this number will not change — it is the object's fingerprint. Two different objects will never have the same id() at the same point in time. The type() function, on the other hand, tells you exactly what kind of object you are working with — whether it is an int, a str, a list, or anything else.

x = 42
name = "Alice"
items = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(x))        # e.g. 140245637849232
print(id(name))     # e.g. 140245602310576
print(id(items))    # e.g. 140245601894784
print(type(x))      # <class 'int'>
print(type(name))   # <class 'str'>
print(type(items))  # <class 'list'>

One of the most illuminating things you can do is check whether two variables actually point to the same object in memory or just hold equal values. Python provides two tools for this: == checks if values are equal, while is checks if two variables refer to the exact same object (same id()).

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
c = a
print(a == b)   # True  — same values
print(a is b)   # False — different objects in memory
print(a is c)   # True  — c points to the exact same object as a
print(id(a))    # e.g. 140245601894784
print(id(b))    # e.g. 140245601895104  <-- different!
print(id(c))    # e.g. 140245601894784  <-- same as a

This distinction between == and is is not just academic — it is central to understanding mutability. When you write c = a, you are not creating a copy of the list. You are creating a second variable that points to the same list object in memory. Any change made through c will be visible through a as well. This is one of the most common sources of unexpected behavior for Python beginners, and it is a direct consequence of how Python's object model works.

Python also has a clever optimization for small integers (typically from -5 to 256) and interned strings. Because these values are used so frequently, Python pre-creates them and reuses the same objects rather than creating new ones each time. This is why the following produces True:

a = 100
b = 100
print(a is b)   # True — Python reuses the same int object for small numbers
x = 1000
y = 1000
print(x is y)   # False — large integers get new objects each time

Mutable Objects — Objects That Can Change

A mutable object is one whose internal state — its contents or value — can be changed after it has been created, without creating a new object. The object’s identity (its id()) remains the same even as its value changes. In Python, the primary mutable types are: list, dict, set, bytearray, and instances of user-defined classes (by default).

Lists are the most commonly used mutable type, and they demonstrate this concept beautifully:

my_list = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(my_list))   # e.g. 140245601894784
print(my_list)       # [1, 2, 3]
my_list.append(4)
my_list[0] = 99
print(id(my_list))   # 140245601894784  <-- SAME id!
print(my_list)       # [99, 2, 3, 4]

Notice that even though the content of the list changed dramatically — we modified an element and added a new one — the id() of the list object did not change. It is the same object in memory, just with different contents. This is the essence of mutability.

Dictionaries work the same way. You can add, remove, or update key-value pairs freely:

person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
print(id(person))    # e.g. 140245601922432
person["city"] = "New York"
person["age"] = 31
print(id(person))    # 140245601922432  <-- still the same object
print(person)        # {'name': 'Alice', 'age': 31, 'city': 'New York'}

Sets are also mutable — you can add and remove elements from them after creation:

fruits = {"apple", "banana"}
fruits.add("cherry")
fruits.discard("banana")
print(fruits)   # {'apple', 'cherry'}

The mutability of these types is what makes them so useful for building data structures that evolve over the course of your program. However, this power comes with a responsibility: you must be careful about who holds a reference to a mutable object, because any of them can modify the shared state.

Immutable Objects — Objects That Cannot Change

An immutable object is one whose value cannot be changed after it is created. If you want a “new” value, Python creates an entirely new object in memory with a new id(). The original object is left untouched. Python's immutable types include: int, float, str, tuple, bool, frozenset, and bytes.

Strings are a great example. Even though Python gives you many powerful string methods, every single one of them returns a new string object rather than modifying the original:

greeting = "hello"
print(id(greeting))   # e.g. 140245602310576
new_greeting = greeting.upper()
print(id(greeting))      # 140245602310576   <-- unchanged
print(id(new_greeting))  # 140245602318128   <-- brand new object
print(greeting)          # hello             <-- original untouched
print(new_greeting)      # HELLO

If you try to directly modify a string character by character, Python will raise a TypeError:

s = "hello"
s[0] = "H"   # TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

This is not Python being restrictive for no reason — it is by design. Immutability makes strings safe to share across your program. If one part of your code holds a reference to a string, you never need to worry that another part of the code will secretly change it.

Integers and floats behave the same way. When you do arithmetic on an integer, Python creates a new integer object:

n = 10
print(id(n))   # e.g. 140245637849232
n = n + 5
print(id(n))   # e.g. 140245637849392   <-- different object entirely!
print(n)       # 15

What looks like “changing n” is actually Python creating a new int object with the value 15 and rebinding the variable n to point to this new object. The original int object with value 10 still exists in memory (at least briefly, until Python's garbage collector reclaims it).

Tuples are immutable sequences — like lists, but fixed:

coords = (10, 20, 30)
# coords[0] = 99   # TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
# You must create a new tuple entirely
new_coords = (99,) + coords[1:]
print(new_coords)   # (99, 20, 30)
print(coords)       # (10, 20, 30)  <-- untouched

There is one nuance worth noting: a tuple itself is immutable, but if it contains a mutable object (like a list), that inner object can still be modified:

t = (1, 2, [3, 4])
t[2].append(5)
print(t)   # (1, 2, [3, 4, 5])  <-- the tuple "changed"... sort of

The tuple t still holds the same three elements (the same references). The tuple itself did not change — but the list object it references did, because lists are mutable. The id() of the tuple remains the same.

Why Does It Matter? How Python Treats Mutables and Immutables Differently

Understanding mutability is not just a theoretical exercise. It directly affects how you write safe and efficient Python code, and Python itself takes mutability into account in several important places.

Memory efficiency. Because immutable objects cannot change, Python can safely share them. Small integers (-5 to 256) and short strings are “interned” — Python creates them once and reuses the same objects throughout your program. This saves memory and speeds up equality comparisons. Mutable objects like lists cannot be shared this way, because sharing them would mean one piece of code could accidentally affect another.

Hashability. In Python, only immutable objects are hashable by default. Hashable means they can be used as dictionary keys or as elements in a set. This makes perfect sense: if you used a list as a dictionary key and then changed the list, Python would have no way to find the key again, because the hash would have changed.

# Immutable types work as dict keys and set elements
my_dict = {(1, 2): "a point", "name": "Alice", 42: True}
# Mutable types CANNOT be used as dict keys
# my_dict = {[1, 2]: "a point"}   # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
valid_set = {1, "hello", (1, 2)}         # all immutable — works fine
# invalid_set = {[1, 2], [3, 4]}         # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

The += operator difference. This is a subtle but important one. For mutable objects, += modifies the object in place. For immutable objects, it creates a new object:

# Mutable: += modifies in place
a = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(a))     # e.g. 140245601894784
a += [4, 5]
print(id(a))     # 140245601894784  <-- SAME object, modified in place
# Immutable: += creates a new object
b = "hello"
print(id(b))     # e.g. 140245602310576
b += " world"
print(id(b))     # 140245602319104  <-- NEW object

Copying. Because mutable objects are shared by reference, copying them requires extra thought. A simple assignment (c = a) does not copy a list — it creates a second reference to the same list. To get a real independent copy, you need to use copy() or slice notation for a shallow copy, or copy.deepcopy() for a fully independent deep copy:

import copy
original = [1, 2, [3, 4]]
shallow = original.copy()         # or original[:]
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
original[2].append(99)
print(original)   # [1, 2, [3, 4, 99]]
print(shallow)    # [1, 2, [3, 4, 99]]  <-- affected! inner list is shared
print(deep)       # [1, 2, [3, 4]]      <-- fully independent

How Arguments Are Passed to Functions

This is where mutability has its most dramatic practical consequences. Python uses a model called “pass by object reference” (sometimes called “pass by assignment”). When you pass an argument to a function, Python does not copy the value. It passes a reference to the same object in memory. The function parameter becomes a new variable that points to the same object as the argument you passed.

What this means in practice depends entirely on whether the object is mutable or immutable.

With immutable objects, the function receives a reference, but since the object cannot be changed, any “modification” inside the function simply creates a new local object. The original variable outside the function is completely unaffected:

def double(n):
    print(f"Inside function, id before: {id(n)}")
    n = n * 2
    print(f"Inside function, id after:  {id(n)}")
    return n
x = 10
print(f"Before call, id of x: {id(x)}")
result = double(x)
print(f"After call, x is still: {x}")   # 10 — unchanged!
print(f"Result: {result}")              # 20
Before call, id of x:         140245637849232
Inside function, id before:   140245637849232
Inside function, id after:    140245637849392   <-- new object inside function
After call, x is still: 10
Result: 20

With mutable objects, the function receives a reference to the same object. If the function modifies the object’s contents (using methods like .append(), .update(), etc.), those modifications are visible outside the function, because both the caller and the function are looking at the same object in memory:

def add_item(my_list, item):
    my_list.append(item)   # modifies the original object directly
fruits = ["apple", "banana"]
print(f"Before: {fruits}")
print(f"id: {id(fruits)}")
add_item(fruits, "cherry")
print(f"After: {fruits}")    # ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']  <-- changed!
print(f"id: {id(fruits)}")   # same id — same object was modified

However, if the function reassigns the parameter entirely (rather than modifying it in place), the original variable is still unaffected. This is because reassignment just points the local variable to a new object — it does not affect the original binding:

def replace_list(my_list):
    my_list = [99, 100, 101]   # rebinding, not modifying
    print(f"Inside function: {my_list}")
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
replace_list(numbers)
print(f"Outside function: {numbers}")   # [1, 2, 3] — unchanged!

This distinction between mutating (modifying the object’s content) and rebinding (pointing the variable to a new object) is the key to understanding Python’s argument passing model. Mutating affects the caller; rebinding does not.

Here is a practical example showing both behaviors side by side:

def process(data, label):
    data.append("new item")   # mutates — caller WILL see this
    label = label.upper()     # rebinds — caller will NOT see this
my_list = ["original"]
my_str = "hello"
process(my_list, my_str)
print(my_list)   # ['original', 'new item']  <-- changed
print(my_str)    # hello                     <-- unchanged

To protect a mutable object from being modified inside a function, you can pass a copy instead:

process(my_list.copy(), my_str)   # function gets its own copy — original safe

Key Takeaways

Understanding how Python handles objects, mutability, and references is one of those foundational insights that changes how you read and write code. Here is a concise summary of everything covered:

Everything in Python is an object. Every value has an identity (id()), a type (type()), and a value. Even None, True, and False are objects.

Mutable objects (list, dict, set, custom classes) can have their contents changed after creation. The object's identity stays the same.

Immutable objects (int, float, str, tuple, bool, frozenset) cannot be changed after creation. Any "modification" produces a new object with a new identity.

Only immutable objects are hashable, which is why only they can serve as dictionary keys or set elements.

Python passes arguments by object reference. With mutable objects, functions can modify the original. With immutable objects, functions can only create new local objects — the caller’s variable is unaffected.

Rebinding (x = something_new) and mutating (x.append(something)) are fundamentally different. Rebinding only affects the local variable; mutating affects the shared object.

When you need a true independent copy of a mutable object, use copy() for shallow copies and copy.deepcopy() for deep copies.

These concepts appear everywhere in real Python code — in function design, data structure choices, concurrency, performance optimization, and debugging. Once you internalize them, a whole class of confusing Python behaviors simply disappears, replaced by a clear mental model of exactly what your code is doing.

Thank you for reading! If this helped clarify Python’s object model for you, consider sharing it with someone who is just getting started with Python. Understanding these fundamentals early makes everything else much easier.

— Written as part of the ALX/Holberton Python curriculum, Project #29
